senses.d: Any long (and possibly endless) era of universal happiness, peace, and prosperity, predicted by various people to come about someday.

From Middle English mylne, mille, from Old English mylen, from Proto-West Germanic *mulīnu (“mill”), from Late Latin molīna, molīnum, molīnus (“mill”), from Latin molō (“grind, mill”, verb), closely allied to Proto-Germanic *muljaną (“to crush, grind”) (see English millstone). Perhaps cognate with Milne (a surname). Doublet of moline, moulin, and blin.
Ultimately from Latin millesimum. The clipping comes by way of the clipped word, millimetre.
Back-formation from millstone, name of a Magic: The Gathering card with this effect (first printed 1994).

senses.d: A grinding apparatus for substances such as grains, seeds, etc. (Some are small and simple, and some are large and complex.)
ex: Pepper has a stronger flavor when it is ground straight from a mill.

senses.d: The building housing such a grinding apparatus; also, any similar building that houses a similarly material activity (such as weaving, fulling, dying, etc.); the place of business comprising such a building and its outbuildings and grounds.
ex: My great-grandfather worked in a mill. He filled the flour sacks and then carried and loaded them.
On Sept. 9 a boiler exploded in Hanke's flouring mill, […]

senses.d: A machine used for expelling the juice, sap, etc., from vegetable tissues by pressure, or by pressure in combination with a grinding, or cutting process; any similar apparatus that otherwise processes.
ex: a cider mill; a cane mill

senses.d: A machine for grinding and polishing.
ex: a lapidary mill

senses.d: A milling machine for machining of solid metal, wood, or plastic.
ex: Several machinists were busy operating the lathes, mills, and drill presses on the shop floor.

senses.d: A milling cutter used on such a machine.
ex: After the drilling and tapping operations, we come in with a mill and do some contouring.

senses.d: A manufacturing plant for paper, steel, textiles, flooring, and some other kinds of materials.
ex: Once the billet gets through the 56-inch mill, it is ready for reheating.

senses.d: The building complex housing such a plant; the place of business comprising such buildings and their grounds.
ex: My grandfather worked in a mill. He operated machinery, did maintenance, and drove forklifts.

senses.d: An establishment that handles a certain type of situation or procedure routinely, or produces large quantities of an item without much regard to quality. (The notion of churning out massive amounts indiscriminately underlies the figurative metaphor.)
ex: Those shysters selling the purebreds are running quite a mill over there, eh?
Getting the book through the editorial mill could take months.

senses.d: An institution or pseudo-institutional business awarding credentials (such as diplomas, degrees, certificates, or certifications) of either dubious value or fraudulent nature; one selling essays or other documents for the buyers (usually students) to fraudulently pass off as their own.
ex: Those shysters cranking out the "IT training certificates" are running quite a mill over there, eh?

senses.d: To grind or otherwise process in a mill or other machine.

senses.d: To shape, polish, dress or finish using a machine.
To engrave one or more grooves or a pattern around the edge of (a cylindrical object such as a coin).
To move about in an aimless fashion.

senses.d: The international mile: a unit of length precisely equal to 1.609344 kilometers established by treaty among Anglophone nations in 1959, divided into 5,280 feet or 1,760 yards.

senses.d: Any of several customary units of length derived from the 1593 English statute mile of 8 furlongs, equivalent to 5,280 feet or 1,760 yards of various precise values.

Cognate with Saterland Frisian moalkig (“milky”), West Frisian molkich (“milky”), Dutch melkig (“milky”), German Low German melkig (“milky”), German milchig (“milky”), Danish mælkig (“milky”), Swedish mjölkig (“milky”), Icelandic mjólkugur (“milky”). Doublet of milchig.

senses.d: Resembling milk in color, consistency, smell, etc.; consisting of milk.
ex: his sword, / Which was declining on the milky head / Of reverend Priam, seem'd i' the air to stick: […]
The Pails high-foaming with a milky Flood,

senses.d: Of the black in an image, appearing as dark gray rather than black.
Containing (an especially large amount of) milk.
ex: milky cocoa    milky tea
Mrs. Anthony, their daily housekeeper, brought in the milky coffee and placed it on the breakfast table.

senses.d: Containing a whitish liquid, juicy.
Cowardly.
ex: Has friendship such a faint and milky heart?

senses.d: Immature, childish.
ex: Gone is your fighting Youth, whom you have bred / From milkie Childhood to the years of bloud!
I am no milky, modest, obedient youth, Constance.

senses.d: Producing milk, lactating.
ex: […] ye heare the Lamb by many a bleat / Woo’d to come suck the milkie Teat:

senses.d: Fighting or disposed to fight; belligerent, warlike.
ex: The upper tiers of the foreign ministry were quick to embrace a militant policy.

senses.d: Aggressively supporting of an idea, group, political or social cause, etc.; adamant, combative.
ex: The physiological state is not itself militant against erotic expression.

From Middle English myllere, mellere, from earlier mylnere, possibly from an Old English *mylnere, from Proto-West Germanic *mulīnārī (“miller”), equivalent to mill + -er; cf. also Late Latin molīnārius (“miller”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Muller, Dutch mulder, molenaar, German Low German Möller, German Müller, Müllner, Danish møller, Norwegian Bokmål møller, Norwegian Nynorsk mylnar, møllar, Swedish mjölnare, Icelandic mylnari. Compare also Middle English milward, mulward (“miller”), from Old English mylenweard (“miller”, literally “mill-keeper”) (> English Millward (surname)).

senses.d: A person who owns or operates a mill, especially a flourmill.
ex: Constable's father, a wealthy miller, operated the mill at Flatford, which still stands 1 mile south of the village.

senses.d: A milling machine.

A floury-smelling mushroom, Clitopilus prunulus.
A rat.
